claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has been reported in a hierarchical-heterostructured state with multilevel chemical fluctuations.
A hierarchical multi-fidelity surrogate combined with targeted active learning can predict Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness for hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10.
The proposed approach can be more efficient than full-scale computational methods while retaining comparable accuracy.
Machine-learning or reduced-order predictors trained on a limited number of high-fidelity calculations can replace much of the large-scale high-fidelity simulation workload.
Active-learning loops can guide sparse experimental validation efficiently.
The surrogate is reliable only in regimes where processing–microstructure–property relationships remain continuous.
The required continuity condition holds when abrupt phase transitions and unforeseen microstructural instabilities outside the training domain are absent.
The hierarchical microstructure mediates stress distribution and deformation mechanisms in HfNbTiVAl10.
Multiscale interactions within the hierarchy connect local chemical fluctuations to macroscopic mechanical behavior.
The proposed surrogate can capture the multiscale interactions associated with the hierarchical microstructure.
Fast low-fidelity predictors can broadly sample the design space, while active learning selectively requests high-fidelity simulations or experiments for outlier correction.
Selective high-fidelity querying can iteratively improve prediction accuracy while reducing computational cost.
The hybrid method can reduce computational cost by approximately 40–60%.
Predictions of Young’s modulus, yield strength, and toughness can remain within roughly 10% of experimental values.
Existing thermophysical calculations, CALPHAD, first-principles methods, and machine-learning models require substantial computational resources and time.
Existing methods have limited predictive reliability for fracture toughness.
The hybrid model will become unreliable in regimes dominated by sudden phase transformations or nonlinear interactions absent from its training data.
In those out-of-domain regimes, the low-fidelity surrogate may omit critical physics and active learning may be insufficient to correct the resulting deficit.
